opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time it felt like a pretty easy decision, but also a slightly scary one. Back in high school I was doing informatics competitions, and through that I got the chance at Tsinghua's offer where they'd lower the admission cutoff by sixty points for me. For a lot of students that's huge. It basically means you don't have to be perfect on the gaokao; you just need to do reasonably well and you're in.

So part of me felt relieved, because the gaokao is this single, very high-pressure exam, and having that cushion took a lot of weight off my shoulders. But another part of me felt like, okay, now I've committed. Taking the reduction meant locking in Tsinghua, and in some cases the major options are narrower than if you just went in with a raw score. I remember thinking a bit about whether I was giving up flexibility.

In the end, though, I didn't regret it. Tsinghua was where I wanted to go, computer science was what I already loved from competitions, and the reduction let me spend my last stretch of high school a bit less anxious. I could still study, still take the exam seriously, but without feeling like one bad afternoon would decide my whole future. Looking back, I think that sense of security actually helped me perform better and enjoy that period more than I otherwise would have.

r001.rationale: The response mentions feeling scared and worries about giving up flexibility, but does not identify uncertainty about the future as the source of that fear.

r002.rationale: The response says she chose Tsinghua because it was where she wanted to go and she loved computer science; it does not attribute the decision to encouragement from her family.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time it felt like a pretty natural decision, even though in hindsight it was a bit of a gamble. The 60-point reduction came through the competition track. I had been doing informatics olympiad stuff for years in high school, and that was the path I knew best. When Tsinghua offered it, the question wasn't really "should I take it," it was more "can I actually make the gaokao score work with that cushion."

I remember my teachers and parents being more nervous than I was. Sixty points sounds like a lot, but if you have a bad day on the exam, it can evaporate fast. So I didn't treat it as a free pass. I kept preparing for the gaokao seriously, almost as if the reduction didn't exist, and then treated it as insurance rather than a plan.

Looking back, I'm grateful for it, mostly because it let me spend my last year in high school still doing the things I actually enjoyed, like writing code and competing, instead of grinding only for the exam. That mindset carried over into university. Tsinghua was where I started doing systems and reinforcement learning work, and that eventually led to projects like Tianshou. So the reduction wasn't just about getting in. It kind of set the tone for how I approached learning afterward.

r001.rationale: The response describes the decision as a gamble and says Jiayi wondered whether her gaokao score would work, but it does not identify uncertainty about the future as a source of her fear. It says she was less nervous than her teachers and parents.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute her choice to family encouragement. It says her parents were nervous and presents her competition experience as the reason the reduction felt like a natural decision.
